lesson.title: Atomic Number: The Periodic Table's Organizing Principle
lesson.summary: Atomic number, the count of protons in a nucleus, is the single value that defines an element and dictates its position on the periodic table.
lesson.body:
Every element has exactly one defining property, and it is not color, hardness, or melting point: it is atomic number, the count of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element. Atomic number is given the symbol Z, and it is written as a subscript before an element's symbol, for example the number 6 before carbon's symbol C, or the number 79 before gold's symbol Au. Since protons determine identity, as established when studying protons themselves, atomic number is really just a formal name for proton count, and it is the number printed above each element's symbol on the periodic table.

The periodic table is arranged in order of increasing atomic number, from hydrogen at Z equals 1 through helium at Z equals 2, lithium at Z equals 3, and onward. This ordering is not arbitrary. Elements arranged by atomic number naturally fall into repeating patterns of chemical behavior, because atomic number also fixes the number of electrons in a neutral atom, and it is the arrangement of those electrons that determines how an element reacts, bonds, and behaves. This is why elements in the same column, or group, of the periodic table share similar chemistry: their atomic numbers differ by a fixed pattern that leaves their outermost electron arrangement similar.

Atomic number stays fixed no matter what happens to an atom chemically. Ionize an atom, and its atomic number does not change, only its electron count does, since gaining or losing electrons never touches the nucleus. Bond an atom to other atoms, heat it, cool it, dissolve it in water: none of these ordinary processes change the number of protons in its nucleus. Only nuclear reactions, such as radioactive decay or nuclear fission, can change atomic number, and when they do, the atom becomes a genuinely different element, which is the deeper reason chemists can predict reaction products so confidently: proton count is chemistry's one truly unbreakable bookkeeping rule.

A worked example: an atom with 17 protons has atomic number 17, identifying it unambiguously as chlorine, regardless of how many neutrons it has or whether it carries a charge. Whether you are looking at chlorine-35, chlorine-37, or the chloride ion Cl-, the atomic number is always 17, because all three still have 17 protons. Compare that to an atom with 19 protons, atomic number 19, which is potassium, a completely different element with completely different chemical behavior, even though the atomic numbers 17 and 19 differ by only two.

Atomic number also sets up the next layer of atomic bookkeeping. Once you know an atom's atomic number, you know its proton count and, for a neutral atom, its electron count as well. What atomic number alone cannot tell you is the atom's mass, since mass depends on neutrons too, a quantity captured instead by mass number, the next concept built directly on top of atomic number and neutron count together.
